9.3.

If a counterparty insists on consent rights, the desk should explain that the \"same-or-better\" collateral quality condition and the \"no Margin Deficit\" condition described above adequately protect the Buyer\'s interests. The Buyer\'s credit exposure is unaffected by a substitution that delivers collateral of equivalent or better quality and value, and the Buyer\'s protection against undercollateralization is preserved by the no-Margin-Deficit condition. Consent mechanisms introduce unacceptable operational delay --- particularly in cross-border transactions where the Buyer\'s credit and operations teams may be in different time zones from Meridian\'s operations desk --- and serve no legitimate protective function that is not already addressed by the two conditions described above.

**5.2 --- Negotiation Notes**

The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:

> \(a\) European bank counterparties commonly open by requiring Buyer\'s prior written consent to any substitution. This is a standard opening position in European bank playbooks and should not be treated as a walk-away trigger for the negotiation as a whole. Instead, the desk should counter with the acceptable formulation described in Section 5.1 (conditional substitution without consent) and explain the commercial rationale. In the experience of the desk, most European bank counterparties will ultimately accept the conditional formulation after one or two rounds of negotiation.
>
> \(b\) Some counterparties may propose a middle ground in which consent is required only for substitutions that involve a change in collateral category (e.g., from sovereign to corporate) but not for substitutions within the same category. This middle ground may appear reasonable but is unnecessary if the \"same-or-better\" condition is in place, as that condition already prohibits downward substitutions. The desk should point this out and insist on the clean conditional formulation without any consent overlay.
>
> \(c\) The 1 business day notice period is operationally critical. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with sufficient lead time to coordinate with the relevant settlement systems --- The Depository Trust Company (\"DTC\") for USD-denominated collateral and Clearstream Banking S.A. for EUR-denominated collateral --- to prepare and execute the simultaneous delivery of substitute collateral and receipt of original collateral. A shorter notice period (e.g., same-day notice) may not provide adequate time for settlement instruction preparation and execution, particularly for EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream, which operates on Central European Time. A longer notice period (e.g., 2 or more business days) may be acceptable if the counterparty insists but reduces Meridian\'s agility in managing its collateral book and should not be offered proactively.
>
> \(d\) The desk should ensure that the substitution mechanics in Annex I are drafted to provide for \"simultaneous exchange\" --- that is, the delivery of substitute collateral and the return of original collateral should occur on the same settlement date and, where possible, through delivery-versus-delivery (DVP) or free-of-payment (FOP) mechanisms that minimize settlement risk for both parties. The desk should not agree to formulations that require Meridian to deliver substitute collateral one or more settlement cycles before receiving back the original collateral, as this would create a \"gap\" period during which Meridian has outstanding deliveries on both sides of the substitution.

**[Section 6 --- Repricing]{.underline}**

Repricing provisions allow one or both parties to adjust the Purchase Price of an outstanding Transaction to reflect changes in the Market Value of the Purchased Securities or changes in prevailing market repo rates during the Transaction\'s term. From Meridian\'s perspective as Seller, in-term repricing introduces operational complexity and potential P&L volatility, particularly where repricing triggers a cash payment obligation (either a payment by Meridian to the counterparty if the Market Value of the collateral has declined, or a return of cash by the counterparty to Meridian if the Market Value has increased). The desk\'s objective is to minimize repricing frequency while acknowledging that bank counterparties with term repo exposures have a legitimate interest in periodic repricing to manage their balance-sheet exposure.

**6.1 --- Repricing Rights**

**Target:** Repricing available only at maturity roll --- that is, no in-term repricing right for either party during the life of an individual Transaction. Under this formulation, the Purchase Price set at the inception of a Transaction would remain fixed throughout the Transaction\'s term, and any adjustment to pricing would occur only when the Transaction matures and is rolled into a new Transaction (if applicable). This target position eliminates the operational burden of in-term repricing and provides Meridian with pricing certainty for the duration of each Transaction.

**Acceptable:** Quarterly repricing or repricing on the 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date, whichever occurs later, with no less than 2 business days\' prior written notice by the requesting party. The desk may agree to either a quarterly cycle (i.e., repricing on the 91st, 182nd, and 273rd calendar day from the Purchase Date, or the next business day if such date falls on a non-business day) or a 90-day cycle (i.e., repricing on each 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date). Where the counterparty proposes both triggers --- for example, repricing on each calendar quarter-end *and* on each 90th calendar day --- the \"whichever is later\" formulation ensures that Meridian is not subject to repricing more frequently than quarterly. The desk should insist on this qualifier in all cases where both triggers are proposed.

The 2 business day notice period is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with adequate time to source replacement collateral, adjust positions, prepare cash for any repricing payment, and coordinate with settlement systems. The 2 business day period also allows for at least one full business day of internal processing after receipt of the repricing notice, accounting for the possibility that the notice is received near end-of-day.

**Walk-away:** Any repricing frequency more often than quarterly --- including but not limited to monthly repricing, bi-weekly repricing, weekly repricing, or on-demand repricing at the counterparty\'s sole discretion --- is not acceptable. In-term repricing at sub-quarterly frequency imposes significant operational and P&L volatility on the desk and is disproportionate to the counterparty\'s legitimate risk management needs. Sub-quarterly repricing must be escalated under the walk-away procedures described in Section 9, and approval is expected to be granted only in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., a transaction with an unusually long tenor and unusual collateral characteristics that justify more frequent adjustments).

**6.2 --- Negotiation Notes**

The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:

> \(a\) Bank counterparties conducting term trades in excess of 60 calendar days will uniformly resist Meridian\'s target of repricing only at maturity roll. The desk should expect to concede this point early in the negotiation and move promptly to the acceptable position. Protracted insistence on the \"repricing at maturity only\" target in the face of clear counterparty resistance is unlikely to be productive and may consume negotiation capital that is better deployed on other issues.
>
> \(b\) The critical protection for Meridian in the acceptable position is the 2 business day notice period. This notice period provides adequate time for the desk to source replacement collateral, calculate and prepare any cash payment, and execute settlement instructions. Do not agree to notice periods shorter than 2 business days under any circumstances. A 1 business day notice period --- or, worse, a \"same-day\" notice period --- would compress Meridian\'s operational response time below acceptable levels, particularly for repricing events that involve EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream.
>
> \(c\) Where the counterparty\'s opening position is a 90th calendar day repricing option (as is common under European bank playbooks, particularly for Swiss and German bank counterparties), a reasonable compromise is to accept the 90th day trigger but add the quarterly alternative, with the \"whichever is later\" qualifier, to smooth timing and ensure that repricing does not occur more frequently than once per quarter. This compromise gives the counterparty its preferred 90-day trigger while protecting Meridian against the possibility that the 90-day cycle and the quarterly cycle could produce overlapping repricing events in quick succession.
>
> \(d\) The desk should be aware that some counterparties may propose repricing triggers that are linked to external events rather than fixed time periods --- for example, repricing upon a credit downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer, a specified decline in the Market Value of the collateral, or a significant move in benchmark repo rates. Such event-driven repricing triggers are generally unacceptable because they introduce uncertainty about the timing and frequency of repricing and can result in multiple repricing events in a short period during market stress. The desk should resist event-driven triggers and should propose that the counterparty\'s concerns be addressed through the margin provisions (which already provide for collateral adjustment in response to market value changes) rather than through the repricing mechanism.

**[Section 7 --- Events of Default]{.underline}**

Events of Default provisions define the circumstances under which a party\'s obligations under the GMRA or MRA may be accelerated and the close-out netting mechanism invoked. Properly calibrated Events of Default are essential both to protect Meridian against a counterparty\'s creditworthiness deterioration and to prevent Meridian from being subject to premature or unjustified close-out by the counterparty. The two Events of Default that are most frequently the subject of negotiation are the Cross-Default provision and the Act of Insolvency grace period.

**7.1 --- Cross-Default**

The Cross-Default provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that a default by a party under any other agreement (typically, a default in payment of indebtedness above a specified threshold) constitutes an Event of Default under the GMRA or MRA, even if no default has occurred under the GMRA or MRA itself. Cross-Default provisions are a standard feature of GMRA and MRA documentation and serve as an early-warning mechanism --- they permit the non-defaulting party to close out and exercise its netting rights before the defaulting party\'s financial condition deteriorates further. However, the Cross-Default threshold must be set at a level that captures only material defaults; a threshold that is too low can trigger cascading defaults across Meridian\'s entire agreement portfolio in response to minor or technical payment failures.

**Target:** Cross-Default threshold of \$50,000,000 for both parties. At Meridian\'s audited net capital of \$412,000,000 (31 December 2024), \$50,000,000 represents approximately 12.14% of net capital --- a level that captures only material payment failures and is well above the range of routine mark-to-market fluctuations, operational payment delays, and minor settlement failures that can occur in the ordinary course of Meridian\'s business. The \$50,000,000 target is Meridian\'s preferred opening position and should be included in all first drafts.

**Floor (Acceptable):** \$25,000,000. This represents approximately 6.07% of Meridian\'s net capital. The desk may agree to any cross-default threshold at or above \$25,000,000 without CFO sign-off. A \$25,000,000 threshold is a reasonable compromise that still provides a meaningful buffer against cascading defaults triggered by non-material events. The desk should offer \$25,000,000 as a midpoint counter-offer early in the negotiation when the counterparty opens below the target, with the goal of closing on this figure and avoiding a protracted back-and-forth on the cross-default issue.

**CFO Sign-off Required:** Any cross-default threshold below \$25,000,000 but at or above \$15,000,000 requires the prior written approval of Meridian\'s Chief Financial Officer. Requests for CFO approval must be submitted in writing (email to the CFO with copies to the Managing Director and the General Counsel) and must include a memorandum setting out:

> \(a\) The counterparty\'s rationale for seeking a threshold below \$25,000,000 --- including any regulatory, risk management, or credit policy considerations cited by the counterparty;
>
> \(b\) The number and aggregate notional of existing agreements in Meridian\'s documentation portfolio with cross-default thresholds below \$25,000,000, together with a list of the relevant counterparties and the applicable threshold for each agreement. This information is necessary to assess the aggregate cascading-default risk across Meridian\'s portfolio --- if a material number of existing agreements already have low cross-default thresholds, the incremental risk of adding another such agreement is magnified;
>
> \(c\) The incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital impact, if any, of a lower cross-default threshold. While the cross-default threshold itself does not directly generate a net capital charge, a lower threshold increases the probability of an Event of Default being triggered, which could in turn require Meridian to take reserves or charges against its net capital computation in connection with close-out or unwind scenarios; and
>
> \(d\) The desk\'s recommendation, including any proposed conditions or mitigants (e.g., a higher threshold that applies only to Meridian\'s obligations, or a cure period that applies before the Cross-Default is triggered).

**Walk-away:** Any cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 is not acceptable under any circumstances. At \$15,000,000, the threshold would represent less than 3.64% of Meridian\'s audited net capital --- a level at which routine mark-to-market losses, minor operational payment failures, or ordinary-course settlement disputes could trigger cascading defaults across Meridian\'s agreement portfolio. The systemic risk to Meridian of a low cross-default threshold is disproportionate to the incremental credit protection it provides to the counterparty, particularly given that the counterparty\'s primary protection in a repo transaction is the collateral itself, supplemented by margin provisions. Negotiators must not agree to a cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 even with escalation; this is a hard walk-away, and no override is available. If a counterparty refuses to accept a threshold at or above \$15,000,000, the desk should inform the General Counsel and the Managing Director, and the negotiation should be paused pending a senior-level commercial discussion about whether the counterparty relationship can proceed on other terms.

**7.2 --- Cross-Default Negotiation Notes**

The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:

> \(a\) European bank counterparties with large CET1 capital bases --- for example, Voss Bank AG, which reported CET1 of CHF 8,300,000,000 as of 31 December 2024 --- routinely propose low cross-default thresholds, often in the range of \$10,000,000 to \$15,000,000. The rationale cited by such counterparties is that these amounts are immaterial relative to their own balance sheets and that their standard credit playbooks require low thresholds for non-bank counterparties. The desk should explain to such counterparties that the cross-default threshold must be calibrated to Meridian\'s capital base, not the counterparty\'s. A \$10,000,000 threshold that is immaterial to a bank with CHF 8,300,000,000 in CET1 capital is manifestly not immaterial to a broker-dealer with \$412,000,000 in net capital, and the cascading-default risk of a \$10,000,000 threshold is borne entirely by Meridian. This is a straightforward and well-understood argument, and most European bank counterparties will accept it when presented clearly and early in the negotiation.
>
> \(b\) Offer the \$25,000,000 midpoint as a compromise early in the negotiation to avoid protracted discussion on this issue. Cross-default threshold negotiations can consume disproportionate time and attention relative to their commercial significance, and the desk is better served by closing on this point quickly at \$25,000,000 and reserving its negotiation capital for issues such as substitution rights and repricing.
>
> \(c\) The desk should be alert to counterparty proposals that define \"indebtedness\" broadly for purposes of the Cross-Default provision --- for example, proposals that include trade payables, margin obligations under other agreements, or contingent liabilities (such as guarantees) within the definition of \"indebtedness.\" The desk should resist such expansive definitions and should insist that \"indebtedness\" for Cross-Default purposes be limited to borrowed money and debt securities, which is the standard GMRA formulation. An expansive definition of \"indebtedness\" effectively lowers the functional cross-default threshold by increasing the universe of obligations that can trigger the provision.
>
> \(d\) Where the counterparty proposes a \"cross-acceleration\" provision rather than a true \"cross-default\" provision, the desk may consider this as a more favorable alternative, as cross-acceleration requires not merely a default under the other agreement but an actual acceleration of the obligations under that agreement. Cross-acceleration provides the counterparty with less aggressive protection than cross-default (because a default may exist for some time before acceleration occurs), but it is commercially reasonable and reduces the risk of cascading defaults triggered by technical or curable defaults. The desk may offer cross-acceleration as a compromise if the counterparty resists the \$25,000,000 cross-default threshold.

**7.3 --- Act of Insolvency Grace Period**

The Act of Insolvency provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that the occurrence of certain insolvency-related events --- including the filing of a bankruptcy petition (whether voluntary or involuntary), the appointment of a receiver or liquidator, the making of an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or the admission in writing of an inability to pay debts as they come due --- constitutes an Event of Default. The key negotiation issue is whether the Act of Insolvency Event of Default is triggered immediately upon the occurrence of the insolvency event or whether the affected party is entitled to a grace period to cure the event before it ripens into an Event of Default.

**Target:** 30 calendar days\' grace period for curing an Act of Insolvency. Under this formulation, the occurrence of an insolvency-related event does not constitute an immediate Event of Default if the event is cured, dismissed, or vacated within 30 calendar days. A 30-calendar-day grace period provides Meridian with substantial time to respond to an involuntary bankruptcy petition (which may be frivolous or unfounded), to correct an administrative error in a regulatory filing, or to take other appropriate action to resolve the insolvency event. This target is aggressive and is unlikely to be accepted by most bank counterparties without significant concession, but it establishes a strong opening position.

**Acceptable:** 10 to 15 business days. The desk may agree to any grace period within this range without escalation. A 15 business day period is the preferred position within the acceptable range and should be the desk\'s counter-offer when the counterparty opens at zero days (immediate Event of Default) or at a grace period shorter than 10 business days. A 10 business day period is the floor of the acceptable range and should be agreed to only after the counterparty has demonstrated clear resistance to 15 business days. At 10 business days, Meridian would have approximately two calendar weeks (accounting for weekends and assuming no intervening holidays) to respond to an insolvency event, which is the minimum period that the General Counsel considers adequate for a meaningful response --- including engagement of bankruptcy counsel, preparation and filing of a motion to dismiss an involuntary petition, and coordination with regulatory authorities.

**Walk-away:** Any grace period shorter than 5 business days is not acceptable. A zero-day grace period --- that is, an immediate Event of Default upon the occurrence of an Act of Insolvency with no opportunity to cure --- is a hard walk-away. Such provisions expose Meridian to the risk that an administrative error in an insolvency-related filing, a frivolous or vexatious involuntary bankruptcy petition filed by a disgruntled creditor, or a technical event that satisfies the definition of \"Act of Insolvency\" without reflecting genuine financial distress triggers an immediate close-out before Meridian has any opportunity to respond, seek dismissal of the petition, correct the error, or otherwise address the situation. An immediate close-out triggered by a technical insolvency event could result in significant losses to Meridian (due to the forced liquidation of collateral at unfavorable prices), reputational damage, and potential regulatory consequences. The 5 business day absolute floor provides the minimum window necessary for Meridian to assess the situation and initiate a response.

**7.4 --- Act of Insolvency Grace Period Negotiation Notes**

The following tactical notes are provided for the guidance of negotiators and outside counsel:

> \(a\) Bank counterparties commonly open at zero days --- that is, immediate Event of Default upon the occurrence of any Act of Insolvency. This is a standard and predictable opening position, and the desk should not be alarmed by it. The desk should counter at 30 calendar days (the target) and expect to settle in the 10--15 business day range.
>
> \(b\) Where the counterparty proposes a bracket --- for example, a 5--15 business day range within which the parties should find common ground --- the desk should push firmly for the top of the bracket (15 business days). Do not accept the bottom of such a bracket if it falls below 10 business days without escalation. Counterparties who propose brackets are signaling willingness to move from their opening position, and the desk should take full advantage of this signal by anchoring at 15 business days and conceding to 10 business days only as a last resort.
>
> \(c\) Some counterparties may propose a differentiated grace period that provides a longer cure period for involuntary insolvency events (e.g., involuntary bankruptcy petitions filed by third parties) and a shorter cure period --- or no cure period --- for voluntary insolvency events (e.g., voluntary bankruptcy filings or admissions of inability to pay debts). This differentiated approach has commercial logic: the counterparty\'s concern about immediate termination is greatest for involuntary events, where the affected party may be an innocent victim of a frivolous filing. The desk may consider a differentiated grace period as a creative compromise, provided that (i) the grace period for involuntary events is at least 15 business days and (ii) the grace period for voluntary events is at least 5 business days. Such a differentiated formulation should be offered only if the counterparty has firmly resisted a uniform grace period within the acceptable range.
>
> \(d\) The desk should ensure that the grace period language is drafted to apply to the \"occurrence\" of the Act of Insolvency rather than to the \"knowledge\" of the Act of Insolvency. A knowledge-based trigger creates ambiguity about when the grace period begins to run and can lead to disputes about when a party became aware (or should have become aware) of the insolvency event. An occurrence-based trigger is cleaner and more certain.

**[Section 8 --- Governing Law, Jurisdiction, and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

**8.1 --- Governing Law**

The governing law of a GMRA or MRA determines the substantive legal framework that will apply to the interpretation and enforcement of the agreement, including the validity of netting and close-out provisions, the treatment of the repo as a sale-and-repurchase trar warranties beyond Meridian\'s standard form (Section 10.4), including without limitation ongoing financial condition representations, material adverse change (\"MAC\") representations, compliance representations beyond Meridian\'s standard \"no conflict\" and \"binding obligations\" language, and any representation that imposes continuing or periodic obligations on Meridian (such as a representation that Meridian will maintain a specified level of net capital or will remain in compliance with specified financial covenants).
>
> \(d\) Walk-away overrides --- that is, any proposal to agree to a term that falls below a \"Walk-away\" threshold identified in these guidelines --- require the joint approval of the Managing Director (Dana R. Castellano) and the General Counsel. Walk-away overrides will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after a written assessment of the commercial rationale, risk impact, and regulatory implications has been prepared and presented to both approvers. The desk should not seek walk-away overrides as a routine matter; the walk-away thresholds are set at levels that reflect the General Counsel\'s and Risk Management\'s considered judgment, and routine overrides would undermine the integrity of these guidelines.

**9.4 --- Hard Walk-Aways (No Override)**

The following positions are absolute hard walk-aways and may not be overridden under any circumstances, regardless of the commercial importance of the counterparty relationship or the transaction:

> • **Cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000** (less than 3.64% of Meridian\'s net capital as of 31 December 2024). As discussed in Section 7.1, a cross-default threshold at this level creates unacceptable systemic risk of cascading defaults across Meridian\'s agreement portfolio. No override is available.
>
> • **Act of Insolvency grace period below 5 business days.** As discussed in Section 7.3, a grace period below 5 business days --- and in particular, a zero-day grace period --- does not provide Meridian with minimally adequate time to assess and respond to an insolvency event. No override is available.
>
> • **ICC arbitration or ad hoc arbitration.** As discussed in Section 8.2, ICC arbitration and ad hoc arbitration are inappropriate for Meridian\'s repo documentation due to cost, complexity, and procedural concerns. No override is available.

If a counterparty insists on any of the foregoing hard walk-away positions and cannot be persuaded to accept an alternative within the acceptable or escalation-subject ranges described in these guidelines, the desk must inform the General Counsel and the Managing Director, and the negotiation must be terminated unless the counterparty revises its position. The desk should not continue to negotiate other terms while a hard walk-away issue remains outstanding, as doing so may create an impression that Meridian is prepared to concede on the hard walk-away point.

**[Section 10 --- Netting, Income Payments, Tax, and Representations]{.underline}**

**10.1 --- Netting**

Paragraph 7(b) of the GMRA provides for the netting of payment obligations between the parties where such obligations arise on the same settlement date and are denominated in the same currency. This netting election is critical to Meridian\'s regulatory capital treatment, as bilateral netting reduces Meridian\'s gross credit exposure to each counterparty and may reduce the net capital charges applicable to repo positions under SEC Rule 15c3-1.

**Standard position:** Paragraph 7(b) of the GMRA is elected. Netting applies to same-currency, same-settlement-date obligations. This election should be included in Annex I of every GMRA negotiated by Meridian and should not be the subject of extended negotiation. If a counterparty proposes to dis-elect Paragraph 7(b), the desk must inform the General Counsel immediately, as the absence of netting has significant regulatory capital implications.

For MRA negotiations, the corresponding netting provisions in the SIFMA MRA should be elected on the same basis --- netting of same-currency, same-settlement-date obligations.

**10.2 --- Income Payments (Manufactured Payments)**

Income payments (commonly referred to as \"manufactured payments\" or \"manufactured dividends\") are payments made by the Buyer to the Seller in respect of income (e.g., coupon payments, dividend payments) received by the Buyer on the Purchased Securities during the life of a Transaction. Under a repo structure, title to the Purchased Securities passes to the Buyer, and the Buyer receives any income paid on those securities. The manufactured payment obligation ensures that the economic benefit of such income accrues to the Seller (who retains the economic risk and reward of ownership).

**Standard position:** Manufactured Payments are due on the next business day following the relevant record date. This one-day lag is consistent with DTC and Clearstream settlement cycles and provides Meridian\'s operations team with adequate time to process and settle the payment. The desk should not agree to same-day manufactured payment obligations, as same-day settlement of manufactured payments is not operationally feasible in all cases, particularly for income payments received late in the business day or in a different time zone from Meridian\'s operations desk.

If a counterparty proposes that manufactured payments be due on the payment date of the underlying securities (rather than on the next business day following the record date), the desk should resist this formulation. The payment date formulation creates a timing mismatch: the Buyer may not receive the underlying income payment until several hours after the opening of business, and a requirement to pay the manufactured amount on the same day introduces settlement risk and operational complexity.

**10.3 --- Tax Gross-Up**

Tax gross-up provisions require the payer of any amount under the GMRA or MRA to \"gross up\" --- that is, to increase the amount of the payment --- to compensate for any withholding tax or deduction required by law, such that the recipient receives the full amount that it would have received in the absence of the withholding or deduction.

**Standard position:** Paragraph 11(b) of the GMRA is elected. The tax gross-up obligation is mutual --- both parties are required to gross up payments to compensate for withholding taxes.

**Cure period:** 5 business days. A failure to gross up within the cure period constitutes an Event of Default. The 5 business day cure period is firm and reflects the General Counsel\'s assessment of the minimum period necessary for Meridian\'s tax and treasury functions to identify a gross-up failure, calculate the correct gross-up amount, and process the required payment. Do not agree to cure periods shorter than 5 business days, as shorter cure periods may not provide adequate time for the identification and correction of gross-up failures, particularly in cross-border transactions involving multiple withholding tax jurisdictions.

If a counterparty proposes to remove the cure period entirely --- such that any failure to gross up constitutes an immediate Event of Default --- the desk should resist on the basis that the cure period is a standard and reasonable provision that protects both parties against inadvertent or technical failures. Tax gross-up calculations can be complex, particularly in transactions involving Purchased Securities issued in multiple jurisdictions, and a reasonable cure period is necessary to address computational errors without triggering disproportionate consequences.

**10.4 --- Representations**

Meridian\'s standard representations in a GMRA or MRA are limited to the following:

> \(a\) **Due organization:** Meridian is duly organized, validly existing, and in good standing under the laws of the State of Delaware.
>
> \(b\) **Power and authority:** Meridian has all necessary power and authority to execute, deliver, and perform its obligations under the GMRA or MRA and each Transaction entered into thereunder.
>
> \(c\) **No conflict:** The execution, delivery, and performance by Meridian of the GMRA or MRA and each Transaction do not violate or conflict with any applicable law or regulation, the organizational documents of Meridian, or any agreement or instrument to which Meridian is a party or by which it is bound.
>
> \(d\) **Binding obligations:** The GMRA or MRA and each Transaction constitute legal, valid, and binding obligations of Meridian, enforceable against Meridian in accordance with their respective terms, subject to customary enforceability exceptions (bankruptcy, insolvency, reorganization, moratorium, and similar laws affecting creditors\' rights generally, and general principles of equity).

These standard representations are pre-approved and should be included in all GMRAs and MRAs without modification.

**Do not agree to the following additional representations without General Counsel approval:**

> • Ongoing financial condition representations (e.g., representations that Meridian\'s financial statements fairly present its financial condition, that there has been no material adverse change in its financial condition since a specified date, or that Meridian is solvent);
>
> • Material adverse change (\"MAC\") representations (e.g., representations that no event or circumstance has occurred that would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on Meridian\'s ability to perform its obligations);
>
> • Regulatory compliance representations beyond the \"no conflict\" representation described above (e.g., representations that Meridian is in compliance with all applicable laws and regulations, including SEC net capital requirements);
>
> • Representations regarding the absence of litigation or proceedings;
>
> • Representations regarding the accuracy of information provided to the counterparty; or
>
> • Any other representation that imposes a continuing or periodic obligation on Meridian, is not within Meridian\'s standard form, or could give rise to an Event of Default based on a condition or circumstance that is not directly within Meridian\'s control.

Counterparties frequently request financial condition and MAC representations as part of their standard onboarding playbooks. The desk should explain that Meridian is a registered broker-dealer subject to continuous regulatory oversight by the SEC and FINRA, including quarterly net capital reporting obligations, and that this regulatory framework provides the counterparty with ongoing transparency into Meridian\'s financial condition that renders additional contractual representations unnecessary and duplicative.

**[Section 11 --- Settlement and Custodial Arrangements]{.underline}**

**11.1 --- Settlement Systems**

The following settlement systems are Meridian\'s standard settlement systems for repo transactions and should be specified in Annex I of every GMRA and in the applicable schedule of every MRA:

> • **USD-denominated Eligible Collateral:** The Depository Trust Company (\"DTC\"). All deliveries and receipts of USD-denominated Purchased Securities and substitute collateral should be effected through DTC, using Meridian\'s DTC participant account. DTC provides real-time gross settlement on a delivery-versus-payment (DVP) basis, which minimizes settlement risk for both parties.
>
> • **EUR-denominated Eligible Collateral:** Clearstream Banking S.A. (\"Clearstream\"). All deliveries and receipts of EUR-denominated Purchased Securities and substitute collateral should be effected through Clearstream. Meridian maintains a Clearstream account for this purpose. Clearstream settlement operates on a Central European Time cycle, and negotiators should be mindful of the time-zone differential when agreeing to margin call cut-off times and substitution notice periods.

These are Meridian\'s standard settlement systems and should not be changed without the prior approval of the Operations Department and the General Counsel. If a counterparty proposes an alternative settlement system (e.g., Euroclear Bank for EUR-denominated collateral), the desk must consult with Operations to determine whether Meridian has the operational infrastructure to support the alternative system before agreeing.

**11.2 --- Tri-Party vs. Bilateral**

**Default position:** Bilateral settlement. In the majority of Meridian\'s repo transactions, collateral deliveries and margin transfers are effected bilaterally between Meridian and the counterparty through the applicable settlement system (DTC or Clearstream). Bilateral settlement provides Meridian with maximum control over the timing and composition of collateral deliveries and is operationally straightforward.

**Tri-party arrangements:** If a tri-party arrangement is elected --- whether at the counterparty\'s request or because the commercial terms of the transaction make tri-party settlement operationally preferable --- BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. is Meridian\'s approved tri-party custodian. BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. has been vetted by the Operations Department, Risk Management, and the General Counsel and is the sole tri-party custodian approved for use in Meridian\'s repo transactions.

No other tri-party agent may be agreed without the prior approval of both the General Counsel and the Operations Department. The desk should not agree to a counterparty\'s proposed tri-party agent --- even if the proposed agent is a well-known financial institution --- without first obtaining these approvals. The approval process for a new tri-party agent involves a review of the agent\'s custodial agreement, operational capabilities, insurance coverage, regulatory status, and creditworthiness, and typically requires four to six weeks to complete.

Where a tri-party arrangement is adopted, the applicable tri-party custodial agreement must be negotiated in coordination with these guidelines, and the terms of the custodial agreement must be consistent with the terms of the underlying GMRA or MRA (including, without limitation, the Eligible Collateral categories, haircut levels, margin provisions, and substitution rights specified in the GMRA or MRA).

**11.3 --- Buy/Sell Back and Agency Transactions**

**Buy/Sell Back:** Not Applicable in all GMRA negotiations. The Buy/Sell Back provisions of the GMRA should be disapplied in Annex I. Meridian does not engage in Buy/Sell Back transactions and has not established operational processes or controls for such transactions. If a counterparty requests the application of Buy/Sell Back provisions, the desk should decline and explain that Meridian transacts exclusively on a classic repo basis.

**Agency Transactions:** Not Applicable. Meridian transacts as principal only in all repo transactions and does not act as agent for any third party. The Agency Transaction provisions of the GMRA should be disapplied in Annex I. If a counterparty proposes that any Transaction be documented as an Agency Transaction, the desk must decline and, if the counterparty insists, escalate to the General Counsel.

**[Section 12 --- Base Currency and Regulatory Identifiers]{.underline}**

**Base Currency:** USD (United States Dollars) for all GMRA negotiations. The Base Currency determines the currency in which margin calculations, net exposure computations, and close-out amounts are denominated. USD is Meridian\'s functional and reporting currency, and all GMRA margin and close-out calculations should be performed in USD to avoid currency conversion risk and to align with Meridian\'s internal risk management and regulatory reporting systems. If a counterparty proposes a Base Currency other than USD (e.g., EUR or GBP), the desk should decline and explain that USD is required for consistency with Meridian\'s regulatory capital computations.

**Regulatory Identifiers:** The following regulatory identifiers must appear in Annex I of every GMRA and in the applicable schedule of every MRA:

> • **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI):** 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12
>
> • **Central Registration Depository Number (CRD#):** 298417
>
> • **Employer Identification Number (EIN):** 83-2947561

These identifiers must be included accurately and completely. Errors in regulatory identifiers can create complications in regulatory reporting, trade matching, and counterparty identification, and may delay the onboarding of new counterparty relationships.

**Counterparty identifiers:** The counterparty\'s LEI, regulatory registration numbers (e.g., CRD# for U.S. broker-dealers, BaFin registration number for German banks, FINMA identification number for Swiss banks), and other applicable identifiers must be verified against public registers (GLEIF for LEI verification, FINRA BrokerCheck for CRD# verification, and the relevant national regulatory authority\'s register for foreign bank registration numbers) before inclusion in Annex I or the applicable schedule. The desk should not rely on identifiers provided by the counterparty without independent verification.

**[Section 13 --- Outside Counsel Coordination]{.underline}**

Meridian\'s current outside counsel for repo documentation is **Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP** (\"PAG\"), located at 570 Lexington Avenue, 30th Floor, New York, NY 10022. The primary contacts at PAG for repo documentation matters are:

> • **Rachel S. Okonkwo**, Partner --- Tel: (212) 555-8430; Email: rokonkwo@pryorashworth.com
>
> • **Miguel A. Ferreira**, Associate --- Tel: (212) 555-8447; Email: mferreira@pryorashworth.com

PAG has been engaged by Meridian to provide legal support for the negotiation and documentation of GMRAs and MRAs, including the preparation and review of Annex I and other supplemental documentation, the drafting of counterparty turn letters, and the provision of legal advice on negotiation strategy and documentation risk.

**Scope of PAG\'s authority:** PAG is authorized to negotiate within the ranges set forth in these guidelines without reverting to the desk on each individual point. This authorization is intended to enable PAG to conduct efficient and responsive negotiations with counterparty counsel while maintaining the boundaries established by these guidelines. Specifically, PAG may:

> • Accept or propose any position within the \"Acceptable\" range described in Sections 3 through 8 without prior desk approval, provided that PAG exercises professional judgment in determining the appropriate position within the range based on the counterparty\'s positions, the overall commercial context, and the desk\'s priorities as communicated in the initial engagement briefing;
>
> • Reject or counter any counterparty position that falls outside the \"Acceptable\" range, consistent with the target positions described in these guidelines; and
>
> • Communicate Meridian\'s standard positions on netting, income payments, tax, representations, settlement, and other matters described in Sections 10 through 12 without prior desk approval.

**Escalation obligation:** PAG must escalate any position that falls outside the \"Acceptable\" range before conveying a response to the counterparty or its counsel. Escalation should be directed to Dana R. Castellano (Managing Director) and the General Counsel by email or telephone, with a written follow-up confirming the issue, the counterparty\'s position, and PAG\'s recommendation. PAG must not convey any response to a counterparty on an escalation-subject issue until receiving express authorization from the appropriate approver(s) identified in Section 9.

**Turn draft circulation:** All turn drafts --- that is, all marked-up versions of the GMRA, MRA, Annex I, or other documentation exchanged between the parties during the negotiation process --- must be circulated to Dana R. Castellano and the General Counsel within one business day of receipt or dispatch. This circulation requirement applies to drafts received from counterparty counsel and to drafts prepared and dispatched by PAG on Meridian\'s behalf. Timely circulation ensures that the desk and the General Counsel are aware of the current state of negotiations and can provide input or direction on open issues.

**Billing:** PAG invoices are reviewed and approved by the General Counsel and charged to the Treasury & Secured Funding desk\'s legal budget. PAG is instructed to provide detailed time entries for all repo documentation work, broken down by counterparty, and to identify any matters involving escalation-subject issues in the invoice narrative.

The desk should propose the prior-consent position in all Turn 1 drafts. Counterparties with active collateral management programmes will frequently resist this position, arguing that the consent requirement impedes their ability to optimise their collateral pools. The desk should be prepared for pushback and should use the prior-consent position as a negotiating lever --- conceding it in exchange for concessions on other terms, such as haircuts or margin thresholds.

**[6.2 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**

Voss Bank may accept a **no-consent** substitution framework --- that is, a framework under which the Seller may substitute Purchased Securities without obtaining Buyer\'s prior consent --- where all of the following conditions are satisfied simultaneously:

> \(a\) The Seller provides at least **1 business day\'s prior notice** to the Buyer of the proposed substitution, specifying the Purchased Securities to be withdrawn and the proposed substitute collateral in reasonable detail (including ISIN, nominal amount, Market Value, and credit rating).
>
> \(b\) The substitute collateral must be of the **same or better Eligible Collateral category** as the Purchased Securities being replaced. For these purposes, sovereign collateral may only be replaced with sovereign collateral of the same or better credit quality; corporate collateral may be replaced with sovereign collateral or with corporate collateral of the same or better credit rating and with the same or shorter residual maturity. A \"downgrade\" in collateral category --- for example, substituting corporate bonds for sovereign bonds, or lower-rated corporate bonds for higher-rated corporate bonds --- is not permitted under this framework.
>
> \(c\) At the time of the proposed substitution, there is **no outstanding Margin Deficit** in respect of any Transaction under the GMRA. If a Margin Deficit exists at the time of the proposed substitution, the Seller must first cure the Margin Deficit (by delivering additional Margin Securities or Cash Margin) before effecting the substitution.

If all three conditions are satisfied, no Buyer consent is required. The substitution may proceed upon expiry of the notice period, provided that the conditions remain satisfied at the time the substitution is effected.

This fallback was used to resolve the substitution issue in the Meridian negotiation at Turn 3. Meridian initially proposed a no-consent substitution right with no notice period and no quality constraints. Voss Bank countered with the prior-consent position. The fallback described above --- 1 business day notice, same-or-better quality, no Margin Deficit --- was proposed by Alistair Fenn of Calder Stone Partners LLP as a compromise, and was accepted by Meridian\'s counsel (Rachel S. Okonkwo of PAG) by email on 14 April 2025. This fallback is approved for general use in future negotiations.

**[6.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

The following substitution rights are unacceptable and constitute a walk-away:

> • Any substitution right that permits a **downgrade in collateral quality** --- for example, substituting BBB-rated corporate bonds for A-rated corporate bonds, or substituting corporate bonds for sovereign bonds.
>
> • Any substitution right that permits substitution **during a Margin Deficit** --- this would allow the Seller to withdraw collateral at precisely the time when Voss Bank\'s exposure is already inadequately covered.
>
> • Any substitution right that does not require **at least 1 business day\'s prior notice** --- this would prevent Voss Bank from conducting even a basic assessment of the proposed substitute collateral before the substitution takes effect.
>
> • Any substitution right that permits substitution of collateral with a **residual maturity exceeding 10 years** (for corporate bonds) or with a credit rating below the minimum ratings thresholds specified in Sections 3.1 and 3.2.

**[Section 7 --- Repricing / Mini Close-Out]{.underline}**

**[7.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank elects a repricing / mini close-out option (commonly referred to as a \"repricing\" or \"re-rate\" provision) exercisable at the **90th calendar day** of any outstanding Transaction, or at each **quarterly anniversary** of the Purchase Date, whichever is later. The repricing right allows Voss Bank (as Buyer) to terminate and reprice the Transaction at the then-current Market Value of the Purchased Securities, adjusted for the applicable haircut, with the effect that the Purchase Price and Repurchase Price are reset to reflect current market conditions.

Exercise of the repricing right requires **2 business days\' prior written notice** to the Seller. Notice may be given by email to the Seller\'s designated notice address (as specified in Annex I) or by such other means as the parties may agree.

**[7.2 --- Rationale]{.underline}**

Repricing rights protect Voss Bank against cumulative drift in collateral value on term trades. In a term repo transaction, the Purchase Price is fixed at inception based on the Market Value of the Purchased Securities at that time, adjusted for the applicable haircut. Over the life of the trade, the Market Value of the Purchased Securities may change --- due to interest rate movements, credit spread widening or tightening, or other market factors --- while the Purchase Price remains fixed.

The margin maintenance provisions of the GMRA (Paragraph 4) provide some protection against collateral value decline by requiring the Seller to deliver additional margin when the Margin Deficit exceeds the Margin Threshold. However, margin calls alone may not fully cure mark-to-market exposure on long-dated term trades, particularly where:

> \(a\) the Margin Threshold is set at a level that allows a material margin deficit to accumulate before a call is triggered;
>
> \(b\) the frequency of mark-to-market valuation is limited (e.g., daily valuation may miss intra-day volatility spikes);
>
> \(c\) the collateral has declined in credit quality or liquidity to the point where its Market Value, even after margin top-ups, no longer provides adequate protection; or
>
> \(d\) the Seller is unable or unwilling to deliver margin in response to a call, creating a period of unhedged exposure before an Event of Default is triggered.

The repricing right addresses these risks by allowing Voss Bank to periodically \"reset\" the economics of the trade to current market conditions. In effect, the repricing operates as a mini close-out: the original Transaction is terminated, the net settlement amount is calculated, and a new Transaction is simultaneously entered into at current prices. This mechanism is particularly important for term trades with a duration exceeding 60 days, where the cumulative risk of collateral value drift is most acute.

**[7.3 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**

The preferred position --- repricing at the 90th calendar day or quarterly, whichever is later, with 2 business days\' prior notice --- is also the fallback minimum. Voss Bank does not have a broader fallback range for the repricing provision; the preferred position represents the minimum acceptable level of protection.

Voss Bank may accept a counterparty proposal that aligns with this formulation even if the counterparty characterises it as a compromise or a concession. For example, if the counterparty proposes \"repricing at quarterly intervals with 2 business days\' notice,\" this is substantively equivalent to the Voss Bank position (since quarterly repricing is consistent with the \"90th calendar day or quarterly, whichever is later\" formulation) and should be accepted.

The desk should note that the repricing right is exercisable at Voss Bank\'s option --- it is not an automatic repricing. Voss Bank is not obligated to exercise the repricing right at any particular interval. The right provides flexibility to reprice when market conditions warrant, without creating an obligation to reprice when conditions are stable.

**[7.4 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

**No repricing right at all is unacceptable for term trades with a duration exceeding 60 days.** This is a firm walk-away, and it applies regardless of the counterparty\'s credit quality or the haircut level agreed. The repricing right is a structural protection that is independent of, and complementary to, the haircut and margin maintenance provisions.

Any counterparty that deletes the repricing right entirely, or that confines the repricing right to maturity rolls only (effectively eliminating intra-term repricing), is proposing a position that falls outside Voss Bank\'s risk tolerance. The desk should not agree to such a proposal, even as a concession in exchange for favourable terms on other points.

In the Meridian negotiation, Meridian\'s Turn 2 redline effectively deleted repricing for in-term periods by proposing that repricing be available only at maturity roll --- that is, only when the original Transaction matures and the parties agree to roll the trade into a new Transaction. This was flagged as unacceptable by Calder Stone Partners LLP, and Alistair Fenn communicated a revised Voss Bank position to PAG by email on 4 April 2025. The revised position --- 90th day or quarterly, whichever is later, with 2 business days\' notice --- is within the acceptable range and should be accepted by Meridian at Turn 3.

If Meridian continues to resist the repricing right at Turn 3, the desk should escalate to Henrik J. Lindqvist for a direct conversation with Dana R. Castellano. The repricing right is a non-negotiable structural protection, and Voss Bank will not proceed with the Meridian GMRA without it.

**[Section 8 --- Cross-Default Threshold]{.underline}**

**[8.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred cross-default threshold is **\$10,000,000** (ten million US dollars). This represents the minimum amount of third-party indebtedness that, if subject to default, acceleration, or non-payment at maturity, triggers a cross-default Event of Default under the GMRA. The cross-default threshold applies to both parties (Buyer and Seller) and is intended to provide early warning of a counterparty\'s financial distress by capturing defaults on material third-party obligations.

A low cross-default threshold is consistent with Voss Bank\'s conservative credit risk management philosophy. By setting the threshold at \$10,000,000, Voss Bank ensures that relatively small defaults on third-party indebtedness --- which may be precursors to broader financial difficulty --- trigger the GMRA\'s Event of Default provisions and enable Voss Bank to exercise its close-out and liquidation rights before the counterparty\'s financial position deteriorates further.

**[8.2 --- Acceptable Range]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s acceptable range for the cross-default threshold is **\$10,000,000 to \$25,000,000**. Within this range, the desk may agree any figure without escalation to the Credit Committee.

The following considerations should inform the desk\'s calibration of the cross-default threshold within the acceptable range:

> • **Counterparty\'s net capital or regulatory capital.** A threshold of approximately 5--7% of audited net capital is a reasonable benchmark that ensures the cross-default provision is triggered by defaults that are material relative to the counterparty\'s financial resources, without being so low as to capture trivial or operational payment failures. For Meridian Capital Securities LLC (audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as at 31 December 2024), a \$25,000,000 threshold represents approximately 6.07% of net capital, which falls within the 5--7% benchmark range.
>
> • **Nature of the counterparty\'s other financial indebtedness.** Counterparties with large outstanding bond or loan portfolios may argue that a low cross-default threshold creates an unacceptable risk of a cascade of cross-acceleration events --- where a default under one agreement triggers cross-defaults under multiple other agreements, amplifying financial distress rather than providing early warning. This concern has some merit, and the desk should be prepared to move within the acceptable range to accommodate it.
>
> • **Likelihood of cross-acceleration cascades.** In markets subject to stress, a low cross-default threshold can itself contribute to systemic instability by triggering a chain of cross-defaults across multiple master agreements. The desk should consider whether the counterparty\'s overall cross-default architecture (across its ISDA Master Agreements, GMRAs, prime brokerage agreements, and other trading documentation) is consistent with the threshold proposed under this GMRA.

**[8.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

Any cross-default threshold **above \$50,000,000** is a walk-away. At that level, the cross-default provision becomes commercially meaningless for a counterparty of Meridian\'s size and profile --- a \$50,000,000 default would represent only approximately 12.1% of Meridian\'s net capital, and a counterparty in that degree of distress would likely already have triggered other Events of Default (e.g., failure to pay, Act of Insolvency) before the cross-default threshold was reached.

Thresholds between \$25,000,001 and \$50,000,000 fall within the escalation band. The desk does not have authority to agree a threshold in this range without Credit Committee approval. The Credit Committee will assess whether the higher threshold is justified by the counterparty\'s credit profile, the nature of the trading relationship, and any risk-mitigating factors (e.g., the availability of additional collateral, the existence of a credit support annex, or the counterparty\'s agreement to enhanced reporting obligations).

**[8.4 --- Meridian Negotiation Status]{.underline}**

The cross-default threshold is one of the open commercial issues in the Meridian negotiation. The negotiation history is as follows:

> • **Voss Bank\'s Turn 1 and Turn 2 position:** \$10,000,000.
>
> • **Meridian\'s Turn 2 counter:** \$50,000,000 (at the walk-away boundary).
>
> • **Expected Meridian Turn 3 counter:** \$25,000,000 (the top of Voss Bank\'s acceptable range).

If Meridian comes back at \$25,000,000 in its Turn 3 redline, the desk is authorised to agree without escalation. This figure represents 6.07% of Meridian\'s audited net capital, which falls within the 5--7% benchmark range and is consistent with the cross-default thresholds agreed in comparable GMRA negotiations with US broker-dealers of similar size and credit profile.

If Meridian holds at \$50,000,000 or proposes a figure between \$25,000,001 and \$50,000,000, the desk must escalate to the Credit Committee pursuant to Section 12.

**[Section 9 --- Act of Insolvency Grace Period]{.underline}**

**[9.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred position is **zero days** --- any Act of Insolvency constitutes an immediate Event of Default with no cure or grace period. An Act of Insolvency is defined in the GMRA to include (among other things) the presentation of a winding-up petition, the appointment of an administrator, receiver, or trustee, the filing of a voluntary bankruptcy petition, and any analogous proceeding under the laws of the relevant jurisdiction.

The zero-day position reflects Voss Bank\'s view that any Act of Insolvency --- even a technical or involuntary filing --- creates an immediate and material risk to Voss Bank\'s ability to realise its collateral rights and to enforce close-out netting. In the US context, the commencement of SIPA proceedings against a broker-dealer can result in an immediate freeze on the firm\'s assets and trading activity, and any delay in triggering the GMRA\'s Event of Default provisions increases the risk that Voss Bank will be unable to close out its positions and liquidate collateral before the counterparty\'s assets are placed beyond reach.

The desk should be aware that the zero-day position will meet resistance from virtually all counterparties, and particularly from US broker-dealers, which will argue that involuntary filings (e.g., creditor-initiated winding-up petitions) should not trigger an immediate Event of Default because such filings may be frivolous or may be dismissed before any insolvency proceeding is actually commenced. This is a valid concern, and the desk should be prepared to move within the acceptable range described below.

**[9.2 --- Acceptable Range]{.underline}**

Voss Bank may agree a grace period of up to **15 business days** without Credit Committee escalation. Within this range, the desk should seek the shortest period the counterparty will accept. Typical negotiated outcomes fall between 5 and 15 business days, depending on the counterparty\'s regulatory status, the nature of the insolvency events covered, and the counterparty\'s negotiating leverage.

The following considerations are relevant when calibrating the grace period within the acceptable range:

> • **Involuntary proceedings only.** Some counterparties will request a grace period only for involuntary insolvency proceedings (e.g., creditor-initiated winding-up petitions) while accepting an immediate Event of Default for voluntary proceedings (e.g., the counterparty\'s own filing for bankruptcy protection). This is a reasonable distinction, and the desk may agree a bifurcated grace period structure --- zero days for voluntary Acts of Insolvency, and up to 15 business days for involuntary Acts of Insolvency --- without escalation.
>
> • **Dismissal condition.** The grace period should be conditional on the relevant insolvency proceeding being dismissed or stayed within the grace period. If the proceeding is not dismissed or stayed within the grace period, the Act of Insolvency constitutes an Event of Default at the expiry of the grace period without further notice or action by Voss Bank. The desk should resist counterparty proposals that extend the grace period indefinitely or that require Voss Bank to demonstrate prejudice before triggering the Event of Default.
>
> • **Notice requirement.** It is acceptable for the grace period to begin running from the date on which the Defaulting Party (i.e., the counterparty) gives notice of the Act of Insolvency to the Non-Defaulting Party (i.e., Voss Bank), rather than from the date of the Act of Insolvency itself. This ensures that the grace period does not expire before Voss Bank becomes aware of the insolvency event. However, the desk should insist that the Defaulting Party has an affirmative obligation to notify the Non-Defaulting Party promptly upon becoming aware of any Act of Insolvency.

**[9.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

**Any grace period exceeding 15 business days is a walk-away.** This threshold is absolute and reflects the minimum speed of action required to protect Voss Bank\'s collateral rights in a counterparty insolvency scenario, particularly for US broker-dealers subject to SIPC/SIPA proceedings. The SIPC can initiate a protective proceeding and obtain a court order placing the broker-dealer\'s assets under the control of a SIPA trustee within a matter of days. A grace period exceeding 15 business days creates an unacceptable risk that Voss Bank\'s close-out and liquidation rights will be overtaken by the SIPA process.

Counterparty proposals expressed in calendar days should be converted to business days for comparison, using the convention that one calendar week contains five business days. Meridian\'s Turn 2 proposal of 30 calendar days equates to approximately 21--22 business days and is outside the acceptable range, regardless of how it is characterised.

Grace periods between 16 and 20 business days fall within the escalation band --- the desk must escalate to the Credit Committee before agreeing any grace period in this range. Grace periods above 20 business days are a firm walk-away regardless of Credit Committee view; the Credit Committee does not have authority to approve a grace period exceeding 20 business days.

A bracket of **5--15 business days** has been identified as the likely resolution zone in the Meridian negotiation. Any figure within that bracket may be agreed by the desk without escalation. Based on the negotiation dynamics to date and the positions communicated by Meridian\'s counsel, it is expected that Meridian will propose 15 business days in its Turn 3 redline. If Meridian comes in at 15 business days, the desk is authorised to agree.

**[Section 10 --- Tax Gross-Up]{.underline}**

**[10.1 --- Standard Election]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s standard election with respect to tax gross-up is as follows:

> • **Paragraph 11(b) of the GMRA: elected.** This provision requires each party (Buyer and Seller) to gross up payments made under the GMRA in respect of any withholding or deduction for or on account of tax imposed by the jurisdiction in which such party is resident or organised. The gross-up obligation ensures that the recipient party receives the full amount of each payment as if no tax had been withheld or deducted.
>
> • **Cure period for failure to gross up: 5 business days** from written notice by the aggrieved party to the defaulting party. Written notice must specify the payment in respect of which the gross-up obligation has not been satisfied, the amount of the shortfall, and the relevant tax jurisdiction.
>
> • **Failure to cure within the cure period constitutes an Event of Default.** If the defaulting party does not pay the gross-up amount within 5 business days of receipt of written notice, the failure constitutes an Event of Default under the GMRA, entitling the Non-Defaulting Party to exercise all remedies available under the GMRA, including close-out and liquidation of collateral.

**[10.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**

The 5 business day cure period is a firm position. The desk should resist counterparty attempts to extend the cure period beyond 5 business days. Common counterparty requests include:

> • **Extension to 10 or 15 business days.** Some counterparties argue that 5 business days is insufficient to investigate and resolve a tax gross-up failure, particularly where the failure results from an unexpected change in tax law or treaty interpretation. The desk should respond that the gross-up obligation is a strict obligation, and that the 5 business day cure period provides ample time for a party acting in good faith to remit the shortfall while it investigates the underlying tax issue. Investigation can continue after the cure payment is made.
>
> • **Carve-out for disputed amounts.** Some counterparties propose that the Event of Default trigger should not apply where the defaulting party disputes in good faith that a gross-up obligation exists (e.g., because it disputes the applicability of the relevant withholding tax). The desk should reject this proposal. Disputes over the applicability of withholding taxes should be resolved through the dispute resolution mechanism agreed under the GMRA (see Section 11), but the existence of a dispute should not suspend the defaulting party\'s obligation to make the gross-up payment pending resolution.

The tax gross-up obligation is bilateral --- it applies to both Buyer and Seller. This is appropriate because both parties may make payments under the GMRA that are subject to withholding or deduction for tax (e.g., Purchase Price payments by the Buyer, Repurchase Price payments by the Seller, manufactured income payments, and margin payments).

**[Section 11 --- Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

**[11.1 --- Governing Law]{.underline}**

**English law is mandatory.** Voss Bank will not agree to New York law, Swiss law, or any other governing law for the GMRA. This position is non-negotiable and applies without exception, regardless of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction of organisation, the location of the Purchased Securities, or the currency of the Transactions.

The mandatory English law position reflects several considerations:

> • **FINMA guidance.** FINMA has issued guidance confirming the enforceability of close-out netting under English-law master agreements governed by the laws of England and Wales. Voss Bank\'s close-out netting opinions --- which underpin the capital treatment of its SFT portfolio --- are predicated on English governing law. A change in governing law would require new netting opinions and could potentially result in adverse capital treatment during the period between execution and receipt of those opinions.
>
> • **Market standard.** The 2011 ICMA GMRA is an English-law document by design, and the vast majority of GMRA negotiations in the European and cross-border markets are conducted on the basis of English governing law. Deviating from this standard would insist on the standard position.

The desk should also ensure that the GMRA clearly specifies the obligations of both parties with respect to manufactured payments in the context of a margin transfer. If Margin Securities have been delivered, the obligation to make manufactured payments on those Margin Securities should be addressed separately from the obligation to make manufactured payments on Purchased Securities.

**[Section 14 --- Settlement Systems]{.underline}**

**[14.1 --- Standard Elections]{.underline}**

The following settlement systems are the standard elections for all GMRA negotiations conducted by the London Branch:

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Currency of Collateral**            **Settlement System**
  ------------------------------------- ------------------------------------
  EUR-denominated Eligible Collateral   Clearstream Banking S.A.

  USD-denominated Eligible Collateral   The Depository Trust Company (DTC)
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------

These elections reflect the London Branch\'s existing settlement infrastructure and custodian relationships. Collateral denominated in other currencies (e.g., GBP, JPY, CAD) is not a standard offering under the London Branch\'s current GMRA programme; if a counterparty proposes non-EUR, non-USD collateral, the desk must consult Operations (London) to confirm whether settlement capability exists for the relevant currency and settlement system before agreeing to include such collateral in the Eligible Collateral definition.

**[14.2 --- Tri-Party Option]{.underline}**

Where a tri-party structure is elected for one or more Transactions, Voss Bank\'s approved tri-party custodian is **BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A.** The selection of BNY Meliora reflects the London Branch\'s existing tri-party custodian relationship and the Branch\'s familiarity with BNY Meliora\'s collateral management platform, eligible securities schedules, and operational procedures.

Tri-party is not the default structure under this playbook. The standard structure is bilateral settlement, in which collateral moves directly between the parties\' accounts at Clearstream or DTC without the intermediation of a tri-party custodian. Tri-party is elected only where specifically agreed between the parties and documented via a separate tri-party annexe (appended to the GMRA) and a tri-party custodian agreement (entered into among the parties and BNY Meliora).

The desk should note that the tri-party structure introduces additional documentation requirements, including the negotiation of the tri-party annexe, the tri-party custodian agreement, and the eligible securities schedule. These documents are typically negotiated in parallel with the GMRA itself and may involve separate negotiations with BNY Meliora\'s documentation team. If tri-party is contemplated, the desk should notify Legal and Operations as early as possible in the negotiation process to allow sufficient time for the parallel documentation workstream.

**[Section 15 --- FINMA Regulatory Requirements]{.underline}**

**[15.1 --- Close-Out Netting Opinions]{.underline}**

Prior to executing any GMRA, Legal must confirm that a current (within 12 months) enforceability opinion on close-out netting under the laws of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction is on file. The opinion must be provided by a law firm approved by Voss Bank\'s Chief Legal Officer and must cover the following matters:

> • The enforceability of the GMRA\'s close-out netting provisions (Paragraph 10) under the laws of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction of organisation.
>
> • The enforceability of close-out netting in the event of the counterparty\'s insolvency, including any applicable insolvency safe harbours or exemptions.
>
> • For US counterparties, the opinion must specifically address SIPA/SIPC treatment of repo collateral and the enforceability of netting under the US Bankruptcy Code safe harbours (11 U.S.C. §§ 559, 561, and related provisions). The opinion must confirm that repo transactions under the GMRA qualify as \"repurchase agreements\" for the purposes of the Bankruptcy Code safe harbours and that the Non-Defaulting Party\'s contractual right to liquidate, terminate, or accelerate is protected from the automatic stay.

The netting opinion must be refreshed at least annually (i.e., a new opinion must be obtained within 12 months of the date of the most recent opinion). If a netting opinion is more than 12 months old at the time of execution of a new GMRA or at the time of entry into a new Transaction under an existing GMRA, the desk must not proceed until a refreshed opinion is obtained.

Legal maintains a register of all netting opinions on file, including the jurisdiction, the date of the opinion, the opining law firm, and the expiry date. The desk should check this register before commencing any new GMRA negotiation.

**[15.2 --- Capital Treatment]{.underline}**

The GMRA must include terms sufficient to ensure that reverse repo transactions qualify for securities financing transaction (SFT) treatment under the Basel III framework as implemented by FINMA (Capital Adequacy Ordinance (CAO), Art. 56 et seq.). SFT treatment allows Voss Bank to recognise the collateral received under reverse repo transactions for the purposes of calculating credit risk-weighted assets and leverage ratio exposure, subject to compliance with the applicable eligibility conditions.

Key conditions for SFT treatment include:

> • The GMRA must provide for enforceable close-out netting (see Section 15.1).
>
> • The collateral must be revalued at least daily (which is ensured by the GMRA\'s standard margin maintenance provisions).
>
> • The collateral must be liquid and must not exhibit a material positive correlation with the credit quality of the counterparty (this is ensured by the Eligible Collateral criteria set out in Section 3).

Haircuts below HQLA floors (see Section 3.3) may cause the transaction to attract higher capital charges under the standardised approach supervisory haircut framework. If haircuts approach the HQLA floors, the desk must escalate to Treasury (Zürich) to confirm the capital impact before agreeing the haircut level.

**[15.3 --- Large Exposure Reporting]{.underline}**

Aggregate gross exposure to a single counterparty under the GMRA must be monitored against FINMA large exposure limits. Under the FINMA framework, a bank\'s total exposure to a single counterparty (or group of connected counterparties) may not exceed 25% of the bank\'s eligible capital (Tier 1 capital plus Tier 2 capital, subject to applicable limits).

The Net Exposure Cap set by the Credit Committee for each counterparty is designed to remain well within the FINMA large exposure limit, providing a buffer against fluctuations in exposure due to market movements, new trades, or collateral value changes. The desk should be aware that the Net Exposure Cap is not the same as the large exposure limit --- the Cap is typically set at a level significantly below the regulatory limit to allow headroom for operational and market-driven exposure increases.

If the aggregate gross exposure to a counterparty under the GMRA approaches the Net Exposure Cap, or if the desk becomes aware of circumstances that could cause the aggregate exposure to exceed the FINMA large exposure limit (including exposure under other master agreements, such as the ISDA Master Agreement), the desk must immediately notify Risk Management (Zürich) and the Credit Committee.

**[Section 16 --- Non-Commercial Drafting Mark-Ups]{.underline}**

**[16.1 --- General Approach]{.underline}**

In any GMRA negotiation, the counterparty\'s counsel will typically propose a number of non-commercial drafting mark-ups in addition to the substantive commercial and legal proposals addressed in the preceding sections. Non-commercial mark-ups include, without limitation:

> • Clarifications to defined terms that do not alter commercial substance.
>
> • Conforming changes to ensure internal consistency within the GMRA and Annex I.
>
> • Typographical corrections.
>
> • Notice mechanic refinements (e.g., updating notice addresses, adding email as a permitted notice method, adjusting deemed-receipt provisions).
>
> • Cross-referencing corrections.
>
> • Grammatical and stylistic changes.

These non-commercial mark-ups should be assessed on their merits. While they do not typically raise commercial or risk concerns, they may inadvertently alter the legal effect of a provision if not reviewed carefully. Accordingly, all non-commercial mark-ups are reviewed by **Calder Stone Partners LLP** before being accepted or rejected by the desk.

Where Calder Stone confirms that a mark-up is purely clarificatory and does not alter commercial substance, the desk may accept the mark-up without escalation to the Credit Committee. Where Calder Stone identifies a mark-up that appears non-commercial but may have unintended commercial or legal consequences, the mark-up is treated as a substantive proposal and is addressed through the relevant section of this playbook.

In the Meridian negotiation, 16 of 23 total Turn 2 mark-ups were classified as non-commercial. Of the 14 marks addressed in the Fenn email of 4 April 2025, 7 were accepted (all of which were non-commercial). The remaining 9 unaddressed marks are pending Voss Bank Credit Committee review. Of these 9 unaddressed marks, the desk expects that a number will be reclassified as non-commercial upon further review, with the remainder being addressed as substantive issues in the Turn 3 redline.
